decision: The repository is created as a skeleton whose module contracts throw, rather than as a working slice of any epic.
rationale: The P0 design pack states that P0 implementation waits for BT-G0 and a Work Package with explicit, expiring authority. BT-G0 is unrecorded. A skeleton that tests its own boundaries is buildable without that authority; a contract with behaviour behind it is not. Every exported function therefore throws with a message naming the epic that would fill it.
alternatives: Implement the tenancy module far enough to be useful, and mark it provisional. Rejected: it would create the very claim AGENTS.md section 12 forbids.
Create only directories and READMEs with no code. Rejected: the boundary rules could then not be observed firing, so the repository would carry an untested instrument.
authority: operator instruction to build the repository from the guide, 2026-09-08

decision: The seven dependency rules are generated from modules/modules.yaml into .dependency-cruiser.cjs, and a hand edit of the generated file fails the build.
rationale: The P0.2 design makes the registry, not the checker, the source of the rules, so that swapping the checker is cheap and a module outside the registry cannot import or be imported. The generator has a --check mode that compares the generated files against what the registry would produce now; that comparison is the generation step of negative control 7.
alternatives: Hand-write the dependency-cruiser config. Rejected: the registry would then describe the modules while the config decided them, and the two would drift.
Use eslint-plugin-boundaries instead. Deferred: ADR-001 chooses the checker; the rules are generated, so the switch stays cheap.

decision: The registry reader is a purpose-built strict parser for the registry shape, not a general YAML library.
rationale: It keeps scripts/ dependency-free, which is the pattern the P0.2 design names for the migration lint, and it lets the reader refuse a shape rather than silently accept one. A silent accept of a malformed registry would generate a rule set that protects nothing, which is the failure mode worth spending strictness on. It throws with a line number on any deviation.
alternatives: Add a YAML dependency. Rejected for now: the registry has one fixed shape and the reader must run before install in CI if that ordering is ever wanted.
Store the registry as JSON. Rejected: the file is read by humans deciding module boundaries, and it carries substantial commentary.
authority: P0.2 design, open question 5, the deterministic-script pattern

decision: Ten of the twelve negative controls of the P0.2 design are observed firing on deliberate fixtures; control 6 and every runtime control are recorded as declared non-coverage rather than passed.
rationale: Control 6 is a push straight to main and a merge with a failing check. Its refusal is the evidence, and only a repository administrator can create the protection that produces it, so an agent claiming it would be claiming a human decision. The runtime half of each control needs a running service and a database, and nothing runs. Recording them as non-coverage keeps the evidence honest; recording them as passed would make the whole matrix worthless.
alternatives: Omit the uncoverable controls from the records entirely. Rejected: a gap that reads as an omission rather than a decision is what the Architect stage rule forbids.
authority: AGENTS.md section 9, declared coverage and declared non-coverage

decision: The brokerage module named for the broker policy representation is registered as policy-record, not policy.
rationale: The migration lint refuses a P0 table named for the four domain words the security proof lists, one of which is policy, and ARCH-001 is emphatic that a broker policy representation is not the insurer-authoritative issued contract. The longer name keeps that distinction in the registry itself rather than only in prose, and keeps the module name from reading as the insurer record.
alternatives: Register it as policy and allow-list it in the lint. Rejected: an allow-list on the first row weakens the rule before it has ever fired.
authority: ARCH-001 section 9, data ownership; P0.SECURITY-PROOF control 6

decision: Mutation testing becomes a committed, required check, scripts/mutation-check.mjs, rather than a technique a reviewer applies once by hand.
rationale: An independent review loosened each rule in turn and found four that no fixture caught: rule 5 widened to any public file, rule 5 narrowed to internals, rule 6 narrowed to services, and rule 5b narrowed to modules. Each would have shipped a boundary that looked tested and was not. A one-time review finds today's gaps; a committed check keeps them found, and it fails on a lost anchor as well as a surviving mutation, because a mutation whose anchor no longer exists has silently stopped testing anything.
alternatives: Add the missing fixtures and stop there. Rejected: it fixes the four known gaps and leaves the next one to chance.
Adopt a general mutation-testing framework. Deferred: the rules live in two files with stable shapes, and a targeted list states in words what each mutation means.
authority: peer review of BIZTRUST-WP-001, finding F4

decision: The gates and authority blocks of current-state.json are enumerated in the schema, with each key pinned to the values legal today.
rationale: Both were declared as a bare object, so the two most governance-relevant blocks in the repository were unconstrained. A review erased every gate and forged three grants, including p0_implementation, and the validator returned exit 0. Pinning the enums means recording a gate or widening a grant is a reviewed change to a schema file, which is what an authority record should cost. It cannot be a one-word edit to a data file.
alternatives: Constrain only the key names and leave values free. Rejected: the forgery was in the values.
Add a cross-record rule in the validator instead. Rejected: the schema is where a reader looks to learn what a field may hold.
authority: peer review of BIZTRUST-WP-001, finding F3

decision: The migration lint normalises double-quoted identifiers, refuses an unqualified object name and a search_path change, matches domain words as stems, and walks nested directories. Its docstring now states its real limits.
rationale: The lint distinguished quoting style rather than intent. CREATE TABLE with quoted names matched nothing and passed; an English plural walked past the domain-word rule; an unqualified name matched no pattern at all despite a comment saying it was a failure; and a nested directory was never read. Four of the design's negative controls were defeated by ordinary, legal SQL. The docstring claimed the lint was conservative and would refuse what it could not read, which was the opposite of what it did, so that claim is replaced by the list of what it genuinely cannot see.
alternatives: Adopt a real SQL parser. Deferred: no research names one for this job, and P0.2 open question 5 assumes a deterministic script. The blind spots are now declared instead of implied.
Keep the text check and say nothing. Rejected: a docstring that overstates an instrument is worse than no docstring.
authority: peer review of BIZTRUST-WP-001, findings F1 and F2

decision: The generated configuration is stamped with the SHA-256 of the registry, and --check compares that stamp.
rationale: The header recorded the last commit touching modules/modules.yaml, which was empty before the first commit and never refreshed after, so it read uncommitted permanently. Worse, --check stripped the line before comparing, so the one field recording WHICH registry produced these rules was never checked. A content hash is stable across commits, is comparable, and is what the P0.2 owners table actually asks for.
alternatives: Refresh the commit SHA after committing. Rejected: a commit SHA changes when any other file in that commit changes, so it does not identify the registry.
authority: peer review of BIZTRUST-WP-001, finding F8

decision: A migration control asserts on the lint's MESSAGE, not only on the rule name.
rationale: Mutation testing found two controls that survived their own rule being disabled. A fixture carrying two violations of one rule proves neither: disabling the shape under test left the file still reported under the same rule name, so a name-only assertion stayed green. Each fixture now carries one violation shape and each control names the message it expects. This was a defect in the tests, not in the rules, and it is the same class of defect as an untested rule one level up.
alternatives: Keep one fixture per rule and accept the coarseness. Rejected: it is exactly the failure the suite exists to prevent.

decision: The secret scan reads bytes rather than decoded text, and the registry reader refuses an unknown top-level key.
rationale: The scan skipped anything that was not valid UTF-8, so it was blind to every binary in the tree; a review found a tracked bytecode file holding an assembled token literal the source deliberately avoids spelling. A secret does not stop being a secret because the file around it does not decode. Separately, the registry reader silently ignored unknown top-level keys, so generated_from sat in the file looking authoritative while nothing read it; an ignored field is a lie with a long half-life.
alternatives: Gitignore the bytecode and leave the scan as it was. Rejected: that removes today's instance and keeps the blind spot.
authority: peer review of BIZTRUST-WP-001, findings F10 and F12
